cards.lead: Salt making from brine springs in the eastern Carpathians
cards.name: Salt production at Poiana Slatinei, Romania
cards.summary: Early Neolithic communities in eastern Romania made salt from a spring by repeated firing, the earliest dated salt production in Europe.
cards.description: The Franco-Romanian excavation at Poiana Slatinei-Lunca found a stratified midden of combustion soils and fireplaces, with more than two metres of accumulated deposit from five centuries of salt production. Nine radiocarbon dates from the earliest and best-preserved part of the deposit place the first salt exploitation in the earliest Neolithic. The authors say it is probably the oldest salt exploitation in the world.
cards.origin_note: The article calls Poiana Slatinei the oldest salt exploitation in Europe and probably the world; other early salt works were not checked in the sources opened.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the sources opened say nothing about consequences for preservation or trade.

events.label: c. 6050–5500 BCE
events.statement: Salt exploitation at Poiana Slatinei, shown by Neolithic fireplaces and nine radiocarbon dates, began in the earliest Neolithic, 6050–5500 BC.
events.quote: Clearly, the first salt exploitation emerged in Eastern Europe during the earliest Neolithic (6050-5500 BC).
events.locator: The earliest exploitations dated by C14

sources.title: The earliest salt production in the world: an early Neolithic exploitation in Poiana Slatinei-Lunca, Romania

open_questions: No opened page gave coordinates for Poiana Slatinei or Lunca, so lat and lon are null; add them from a gazetteer or the excavation report.
The article does not give its publication year; check it.

The lead's reasons for salt (preserving meat, fish and dairy) are not in this article, which only asks whether salt was for food, preservation or livestock; compare with the 2018 abstract and other early salt works (Solnitsata, Zhongba) before calling it the world's first.

cards.lead: Stockfish production for export in Arctic Norway
cards.note: The source shows Lofoten-stock cod at the Baltic port of Haithabu in 800–1066 CE, not a Norwegian export fishery by about 1000 CE. The sample is five bones, and the researchers say it cannot show whether the cod was traded or eaten on a voyage. The lead's claim of Europe's first bulk trade and its independence are not supported by the source.
cards.name: Lofoten cod reaching Haithabu, Viking Age
cards.summary: Viking-age cod from the Lofoten fishing stock reached the Baltic port of Haithabu, possibly as dried stockfish carried over long distances.
cards.description: Cod is dried outdoors in northern Norway on wooden frames, and some medieval accounts say stockfish stayed edible for up to ten years. Five cod bones from the wharves of Haithabu, dated 800–1066 CE, carried DNA of the Arctic cod stock that spawns off Lofoten. The researchers say this is the earliest evidence for fish from northern Norway being eaten on the European mainland.
cards.origin_note: The sources show where the cod were caught but not when or where stockfish drying began, so independence cannot be judged.

impact.note: Lowered from the lead's reach 2 and depth 1: the evidence is five bones and does not yet show bulk trade.

events.label: 800–1066 CE
events.statement: Five cod bones from the wharves of Haithabu, dated 800–1066 CE, carry DNA of the Arctic cod stock that spawns off Lofoten.
events.quote: The study analysed five cod bones dating from between 800 and 1066 AD found in the mud of the former wharves of Haithabu

sources.title: DNA from Viking cod bones suggests 1,000 years of European fish trade

open_questions: When did drying cod for export begin in Lofoten? The primary PNAS paper (Star et al. 2017) was not opened and should be read for the full sample and its limits.
Whether the Haithabu cod were traded or were provisions for a voyage, as the researchers say the sample cannot settle.
Coordinates for Lofoten and Haithabu come from a gazetteer, not from the sources cited; verify them.

cards.lead: Roller flour milling in Switzerland and Hungary
cards.note: The Pest roller mill is confirmed as operating from 15 September 1841, earlier than the lead's 1865–1875 perfection date. The Swiss origin (Sulzberger, 1834 in the lead) could not be checked: the Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz and Mills Archive pages were blocked to the fetcher. Mechwart's chilled-iron rolls (1874) are not confirmed from an openable page.
cards.name: Steam roller flour mill at Pest, Hungary
cards.summary: A steam-powered roller mill in Pest, Hungary, began operating in 1841 as the first commercial mill of its kind there.
cards.description: The Pesti József Hengermalom Részvénytársulat, a joint-stock company, built a roller mill in Pest that became operational on 15 September 1841. The company was the first commercial mill based on steam power in Hungary and was rebuilt after fires in 1850 and 1851. The new mill of 1867 was more modern than the one it replaced.
cards.origin_note: The page opened does not say where the roller milling method came from, so independence cannot be judged from it.

impact.note: Scored for this one Pest mill; the lead's reach 3 describes the spread of roller milling as a whole, which this record does not show.

events.label: 15 September 1841
events.statement: The Pest roller mill of the Pesti József Hengermalom company became operational on 15 September 1841.
events.quote: It became operational on 15 September 1841, the same year.
events.locator: History of the company (mill built by 1841)

open_questions: Whether Sulzberger's roller mill at Frauenfeld, Switzerland (1830s) can be dated from an openable source; the lead's 1834 date is not confirmed and the HLS page gives, in the search result, 1832.
Whether the Pest mill used Swiss roller designs or the Bolzano contact mentioned in the museum text.
Mechwart's chilled-iron roller date (1874 in the Hungarian museum text, c. 1870 in Mills Archive) needs a fetchable source.
Coordinates are the Budapest gazetteer point, not the mill site; verify them.

cards.lead: Eye paint and cosmetics in predynastic Egypt
cards.note: The cited source dates synthetic lead-chloride cosmetic powders to 2000–1200 BC, which matches the lead's late claim. The earliest Predynastic malachite-palette date of c. 4400 BCE is not supported by an openable source: the Stevenson article describes malachite grinding in the Predynastic period but gives no year. The Badarian date range is in Wikipedia only.
cards.name: Lead-based cosmetic powders in Egypt
cards.summary: Egyptian makers prepared synthetic lead-chloride cosmetic powders, found in samples dated 2000–1200 BCE.
cards.description: A 1999 Nature study examined cosmetic powders from 2000–1200 BCE preserved in their original containers. It found laurionite and phosgenite, lead compounds that the authors judged to be synthetic products made by Egyptians using wet chemistry. Earlier Predynastic palettes were used to grind malachite, which the Stevenson article links to eye paint.
cards.origin_note: Nature says make-up has been known since the earliest periods of Egyptian history, but the sources opened do not show that it was the first anywhere or whether it was independent.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the sources opened do not show the consequences beyond Egypt.

events.label: 2000–1200 BCE
events.statement: Cosmetic powders dating from 2000–1200 BCE contained lead chlorides that the authors judged synthetic, made by Egyptians using wet chemistry.
events.quote: We have investigated cosmetic powders dating from between 2000 and 1200 BC that were preserved in their original containers.

open_questions: The Predynastic and Badarian date for malachite palettes (c. 4400–4000 BCE) needs a citable source; the Stevenson article gives no year.
The site of the 2000–1200 BCE samples is not in the opened text; find it in the full Nature article.
Coordinates are null for Egypt; a site coordinate is needed for the sample findspot.
The lead's claim that malachite palettes began a cosmetics trade is not in the sources opened.

cards.lead: Polished iron-ore mirrors in Olmec Mesoamerica
cards.note: The source dates the Olmec iron-ore objects to the Early Formative period, 1500–900 BC, not c. 1400–1000 BCE. It says they were plane or concave mirrors up to 10 cm across. Whether they were made independently of the Old World is not shown by the source.
cards.name: Iron-ore mirrors at San Lorenzo and San José Mogote
cards.summary: Olmec craftsmen polished iron ore into small plane or concave mirrors worn on the body, dated 1500–900 BC.
cards.description: Polished hematite or magnetite plates, plane or concave and up to 10 cm across, were made at San José Mogote and San Lorenzo in the Early Formative period. The source says they were apparently used as body adornments and were probably a measure of social status. The iron ore for the San José Mogote plates came from sources about 30 km away.
cards.origin_note: The source does not say whether these mirrors were made independently of Old World examples, so independence cannot be judged.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the source does not show their reach beyond Olmec sites.

events.label: 1500–900 BC
events.statement: Olmec iron-ore mirrors from San Lorenzo and San José Mogote date from the Early Formative period, 1500–900 BC.
events.quote: Archaeologists have found Olmec objects made of iron ore, dating from the Early Formative period (1500 - 900 BC) in sites in San José Mogote and San Lorenzo.

sources.title: Mexico and the early history of magnetism

open_questions: A 2021 Cambridge introduction on iron-ore mirrors (not fetchable) reportedly says the first iron-ore mirrors may be Zapotec, in the Valley of Oaxaca, 1200–850 BC; check it against the San José Mogote evidence.
The La Venta concave mirrors and the obsidian mirrors of Çatalhöyük were not checked.
Coordinates come from a gazetteer, not from the cited source; verify them.

cards.note: The source dates the Tongatapu combs to about 2,700 years before 1950, which is about 750 BCE rather than 700 BCE. It says researchers do not know whether comb tattooing arrived with the Lapita migrants or developed in Polynesia, so the lead's independent origin is not supported.
cards.name: Bone-comb tattooing in Tonga
cards.summary: Tongan tattooists used hafted bone combs and a complete kit about 2,700 years ago, the oldest confirmed tattooing combs in Oceania.
cards.description: A tattooist's kit excavated on Tongatapu in 1963 includes four multi-toothed combs, radiocarbon dated to about 2,700 years old. The combs were made from bone, two from a large seabird and two probably from human bone. Whether the practice came with Lapita migrants or developed within Polynesia remains an open question.
cards.origin_note: The source says it is not known whether comb tattooing came with Lapita migrants or developed within Polynesia, so independence cannot be judged.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the source does not show reach beyond Tonga and the region.

events.label: c. 750 BCE
events.statement: Four tattooing combs from Tongatapu, radiocarbon dated to about 2,700 years before 1950 (about 750 BCE), are the oldest confirmed tattooing combs in Oceania.
events.quote: Radiocarbon dating of the tools found them to be 2700 years old, making them the oldest confirmed tattooing combs found in Oceania.

sources.title: Tools in world’s oldest tattoo kit made from human bone

open_questions: The primary paper (Clark and Langley, Journal of Island & Coastal Archaeology, 2019) was not opened; check its date and comb sample.
Whether comb tattooing came with the Lapita migration or developed within Polynesia is unresolved in the source.
Older tattooed skin (Ötzi and Egyptian mummies, c. 3300 BCE) was not checked in an openable source.
Coordinates come from a gazetteer, not from the cited source; verify them.
